Text | Xiaoyu Niu

Editors | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Introduction

I’m delighted that Fanyu Meng invited me to tell you the story of the “fly microphone.” If anything here is inaccurate, I’d be grateful for corrections. Since this is a popular-science piece, I’ll try to explain the ideas in plain language. Readers who want the details can look up the keywords mentioned here in the academic literature; I’m sure it will be well worth the effort.

1. The “super ear” of the fly Ormia ochracea

There is a fly called Ormia ochracea that lives only in Texas and Florida in the United States. In 1975, biologists discovered for the first time that this fly lays its eggs inside crickets. The larvae eat the cricket’s body as they grow to maturity. A gruesome thought: its own survival comes at the cost of another creature’s life.

For the fly, carrying on the line means finding crickets to lay its eggs in. We often hear crickets chirping at night: they are calling to attract a mate. But the same song also attracts their natural enemy.

What astonished scientists is that the fly can orient toward a cricket from several kilometers, or even more than ten kilometers, away. Purely by “ear”! As we all know, the precision of spatial localization is closely tied to the physical size of the sensor. Roughly speaking, the larger the sensor, the better it can determine direction. Given the size of the fly’s ears and how well it localizes, it is as if we stood in China and used our two legs to tell whether an earthquake on the other side of the world had struck Chile or Argentina.

For us humans, that is clearly impossible.

But the fly can do it!

You could say that, for the same power consumption, the fly’s “ear” is the most sensitive, or most advanced, microphone known to humankind. It makes sense, really: human-made microphones have existed only for the last hundred years or so, while the fly’s “microphone” has been evolving and iterating for millions of years.

2. The physics of the super ear

In 1995, scientists worked out the physics behind the fly’s remarkable ear.

The fly’s ear works differently from the human ear, which has a single mode of vibration. It is a seesaw-like structure with two vibration modes. The first mode (shown above) senses the pressure gradient, and the second senses the pressure itself. Together they naturally achieve spatial adaptive filtering, in other words, directivity.

The human ear, on the other hand, like the microphones in the vast majority of consumer electronics, senses only the pressure itself. That is why it is hard to tell the direction of a sound with a single ear or a single microphone.

And that is the secret of the fly’s ear.

3. Bio-inspired microphone chips

None of the work described so far comes from our lab; our lab’s part of the story begins with the development of bio-inspired microphone chips. From 2000 onward, a number of research groups took up the development of fly-inspired microphone chips. Frankly, progress was very slow. Around 2014, our lab built the first fly microphone using piezoelectric material. This piezoelectric solution was rated by the IEEE as the most practical and outstanding fly-inspired microphone chip. Interested readers can look it up; I won’t go into it here. Michael, the PhD student who came out of this project, was snapped up by Knowles the moment he graduated.

This picture shows the fly microphone our lab made from piezoelectric material. It was taken with a scanning electron microscope, which is why it is in black and white.

This one was taken with an optical microscope.


Measuring the chip’s eigenmodes with a laser Doppler vibrometer showed that the structure reproduces the fly’s two vibration modes. That was exactly what we were after. Measurements of its directivity also showed that a single microphone chip is very directional indeed. I won’t go into the details here.

A quick digression: around 2009, Knowles led the microphone industry past a milestone, when shipments of MEMS microphones overtook those of traditional electret condenser microphones for the first time. But the only MEMS microphones that could be mass-produced were omnidirectional condenser microphones, and that has remained true for more than a decade. Only in the last few years did Vesper, a spin-off from the University of Michigan, become the first company to commercialize piezoelectric MEMS microphones, which gave the whole industry a lift. Piezoelectric MEMS microphones are therefore widely seen as a promising direction for the industry.

4. Applications, outlook and reflections

Directional microphones like this have many applications. The most typical one we are working on now is hearing aids. Conventional hearing aids mostly use omnidirectional condenser microphones, which makes it hard for wearers to pick out one voice in a noisy room, the so-called cocktail party effect. With a directional microphone, that becomes much easier.

Directional microphones are also in great demand in consumer electronics. Our lab has long worked closely with Samsung, though I can’t share any details here. Soldier systems in defense also badly need directional microphones, to determine the direction of gunfire quickly and accurately.

Looking ahead, our lab plans to focus on improving the mechanical design and the piezoelectric material. The first-generation directional microphone, for example, used PZT as its piezoelectric material; for the second generation we may try AlN. That is the work I’m doing at the moment.

I have been working on this project for several months now, and what I think about most is the relationship between humans and nature. Humans are powerful, but nature is more powerful still, and so many of its secrets remain undiscovered. So let us hold nature in awe, and let nature be our teacher.

References

The content above is based mainly on a talk Professor Neal A. Hall gave at a 2021 seminar of the Texas chapter of the Acoustical Society of America (http://www.texasacoustics.org/).

About the lab: The UT Acoustic MEMS Lab at the University of Texas at Austin uses MEMS sensor technology to solve problems in acoustics. Founded in 2009 and led by Professor Neal Hall, the lab has worked on numerous projects funded by the US Department of Energy, the Department of Health and Human Services, the Department of Defense, the US Navy, Apple, Samsung, NASA and others. Its current focus is the development, application and commercialization of acoustic MEMS sensors. Students who love acoustics or MEMS are welcome to join. Lab website: https://sites.google.com/site/utacousticmems/

About the author: Xiaoyu Niu graduated in 2019 with a bachelor’s degree in underwater acoustics from Ocean University of China, then studied under Xiaodong Li at the Institute of Acoustics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, working mainly on coupled reverberation time and dispersion in physical acoustics. In 2020 Niu joined the UT Acoustic MEMS Lab to pursue a PhD in electrical engineering under Neal Hall. Niu’s research interests are the design, development and fabrication of acoustic MEMS transducers, and current projects include a MEMS parametric array loudspeaker and a MEMS directional microphone with multiple coupled modes.
